As a heat wave moves into the Triad, local health and child education experts are sharing tips for keeping children safe in the heat.
Pediatrician Dr. Jaclyn Dovico and child education expert Adam Dovico, co-owners of Joyful Pediatrics, recommend dressing children in layers so they can adjust their clothing as temperatures change.
"I encourage parents to dress their kids in layers, or at least send a sweatshirt or long sleeve shirt to school, because while it's hot outside, inside the school and inside the classroom can be very cold because of the air conditioning, so those extremes can actually be uncomfortable on either end for the child," Adam Dovico said.
Experts also recommend teaching younger children to recognize the signs of dehydration and overheating.
Jaclyn Dovico said children should be reminded to drink water regularly because they may not recognize when they are thirsty.
"Remind children to drink often. They don't recognize signs of thirst and so as a parent or as a teacher it's important to remind them to have drink and take breaks throughout the day, whether it's recess, sports, etc.," she said.
Dovico said younger children can become dehydrated faster than older children.
She also said parents, teachers and other adults should help children recognize symptoms of overheating or dehydration.
"It's important for parents to talk to children about, signs that you're feeling overheated or dehydrated. You are going to get more tired. You're going to be breathing heavier. You're going to have more headaches, eventually some dizziness," Dovico said.
She encouraged adults to teach children to listen to their bodies and tell an adult when they experience those symptoms.
"Children experiencing symptoms should take a break by sitting or lying down," Dovico said. "If they do not take a break the symptoms could lead to heat exhaustion or fainting."
Joyful Pediatrics is different from other pediatrician offices in Greensboro because it offers a direct pediatric care model.
The practice does not keep traditional office hours. Appointments are scheduled based on each family's needs, and families can reach out with questions at any time.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) yesterday issued its highest-level consumer safety alert after US regulators warned that a defect in a temporary heart pump system has been linked to three deaths and 37 serious injuries overseas.
The warning came after the US Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday last week announced that Abiomed Inc, a subsidiary of Johnson & Johnson, was recalling its Automated Impella Controllers due to a cartridge recognition malfunction.
The defect could prevent the controller from confirming whether the cartridge was installed properly, potentially affecting the device’s operation, the US agency said.
Photo: Taipei Times
As of Aug. 17, Abiomed had reported 37 serious injuries and three deaths related to the issue, it said.
The Impella ventricular support system, described as the world’s smallest heart pump, provides temporary circulatory support for people with severe heart conditions, including cardiogenic shock, as well as those undergoing high-risk procedures such as percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass graft surgery, FDA Medical Devices and Cosmetics Division Director Chien Chia-hung (錢嘉宏) said.
Taiwan has one approved product license for the device, which is used by 19 medical institutions, Chien said.
The affected products in Taiwan include 102 purge cassettes, 26 controllers and 97 introducers, the director said.
No injuries or adverse events related to the defect have been reported in Taiwan, Chien said, adding that the devices are used under close supervision by medical professionals.
The FDA has instructed the local license holder, Johnson & Johnson MedTech, to notify healthcare providers of the alert and implement the manufacturer’s corrective measures, including replacing affected components, updating software and bolstering monitoring procedures.
The agency said it has been monitoring safety information on the product throughout the year and issued several notices on its Web site, but none had involved a recall.
The agency’s consumer safety alert system has three tiers: red, yellow and green.
A red alert, the highest level, is issued when products that are available in Taiwan report incidents overseas that involve serious injuries or deaths, or when defects could cause severe harm and require risk-control measures.

But barn owls' sounds are considered the least pleasant, according to the findings.
Their findings show that calls which are varied, higher-pitched and not too loud are considered most pleasant — with blackbird songs topping the charts.
Participants rated the perceived pleasantness of 123 different bird songs on a scale from one (not very pleasant) to five (very pleasant).
The blackbird topped the pleasantness table with an average score of 4.52, just beating the willow warbler (4.45) with the blackcap completing the top three.
The barn owl finished rock bottom with an average pleasantness score of just 1.32.
The German research team explained that identifying what makes birdsong beautiful could improve understand how soundscapes make the natural world relaxing for humans.
They say their findings, published in the journal Frontiers in Bird Science, could help to improve parks, upgrading the design of stressful places such as hospital waiting rooms, and promote conservation through birds with especially lovely songs.
By asking people to listen to birdsongs and rate them for pleasantness, then cross-referencing the results with information about the calls' acoustic characteristics, the scientists identified key aspects that make some birdsongs seem more pleasant than others.
But although people who valued birds more rated songs more highly, knowing more about birds didn't influence perceived pleasantness.
Study lead author Nadine Kalb, from the University of Tübingen, said: "You don't have to be a 'bird person' to find bird sounds beautiful.
"Being able to recognize birds by their appearance or song did not affect how people rated calls.
"This suggests that enjoyment of birdsong is connected to something more fundamental than just knowing what you are listening to."
She explained that pleasantness is a subjective, perceived measure which is affected by personal taste.
The research team suspected that some acoustic characteristics, such as a high amplitude — perceived as a loud noise — would be associated with a lower pleasantness rating.
But they also suspected some personal characteristics, such as individuals' knowledge about birds, would influence pleasantness ratings.
Study senior author Christoph Randler, also from the University of Tübingen, said: "I have been a birder since I was 10, although at that age I didn't know about ecosystem services or acoustic analyses.
"Bird sounds are often considered one of the most enjoyable aspects of spending time in nature, and previous research has shown that they can contribute to psychological restoration and well-being.
"However, not all bird sounds are perceived equally positively."
The scientists recruited 84 people and played them short clips of 123 songs from wild birds commonly found throughout Germany.
Participants were then asked to rate each clip on a scale from one to five — the higher, the more pleasant.
Participants were also asked questions which measured their birding skills and their perception of birds.
The researchers then analyzed the clips, measuring aspects of each song's amplitude, frequency, complexity — the number and variety of elements in the song — and bandwidth, which captured the range of frequencies a song used.
A song with a big difference between its highest and lowest frequencies would have a wide bandwidth.
The data was then cross-referenced with participants' pleasantness scores for songs and their pre-existing interest in birds.
The scientists identified 21 species among their samples which had also been included in a study about perceptions of birdsong as restorative — helping people to recover from mental fatigue or stress.
They compared the ratings these birds received in that study with their pleasantness scores.
A blackbird's song was considered most pleasant while a barn owl's was considered least pleasant.
Blackbirds' songs were also considered highly restorative.
A narrower bandwidth and greater complexity were perceived as more pleasant, as were birdsongs at a higher frequency or with a relatively low amplitude.
The songs that scored highest also avoided a key frequency range where human hearing is highly sensitive.
People who liked birds more tended to rate them more highly, but their level of bird knowledge had no effect on ratings.
Kalb said: "We might be wired to prefer more variable sounds with moderate amplitudes and frequencies because they signal a safe, healthy, and restorative environment where we can relax."
The scientists pointed out that factors they couldn't test, such as call rate — some birds call more frequently than others — might affect perceptions of pleasantness.
To follow up the research, they want to carry out larger studies with broader samples including more men, different cultures and more experienced birdwatchers.
Randler said: "I would love to investigate how bird sounds influence people in real-world environments."
He added: "I would also like to integrate ecological data, acoustic analyses, and psychological responses to understand how changes in biodiversity - like species loss - translate into changes in human experiences of nature.
"That would help us better understand the role that healthy ecosystems play in supporting both biodiversity and human well-being."
